title: Fix 'syntax error near unexpected token' in a shell command or script
summary: This error means bash found a word or character in the wrong place, for example a doubled 'fi' or a missing closing quote. It often happens after copy-paste. Bash shows the line number, so you can check the text without running it and fix that line.

error_patterns: unexpected EOF while looking for matching
syntax error: unexpected end of file
prerequisites: The script file, or the one-line command you tried to run

steps.explain: Check the script for syntax errors without running it. Bash reads the file and stops at the first problem. Look at the number after 'line' in the message: that is the line to fix. No output means the syntax is fine.

placeholders.name: SCRIPT
placeholders.description: The script file that gives the error

steps.expect: Typical output: '<SCRIPT>: line 5: syntax error near unexpected token `fi''. The number 5 is the line to check.

alternatives.explain: If the error came from one command you pasted into the terminal, not from a file, check that text without running it. Put the pasted text in single quotes. If the command itself contains single quotes, save it to a file and use the step above.

placeholders.name: COMMAND
placeholders.description: The pasted command text, in single quotes

alternatives.expect: Typical output for a missing closing quote: 'bash: -c: line 1: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"''.

steps.explain: Print the line that bash reported, so you can see exactly what is wrong. A missing quote is usually reported on the line where the quote was opened.

placeholders.name: LINE
placeholders.description: The line number from the bash -n message

placeholders.name: SCRIPT
placeholders.description: The script file that gives the error

steps.expect: The text of that one line, for example 'fi fi'.

steps.explain: Find characters that copy-paste often brings in, such as curly quotes (“ ” ‘ ’), long dashes or non-breaking spaces. The shell does not know them, so they break commands. Tab characters also appear in this list and are normal.

placeholders.name: SCRIPT
placeholders.description: The script file that gives the error

steps.expect: Lines with a number and the odd character, for example '3:echo “hello”'. No output means no odd characters were found.

steps.explain: Fix the line from step 2: delete the extra word or character (for example the second 'fi'), add the missing closing quote, and replace curly quotes with plain straight quotes. Then save the file.
steps.gui: Open the script in a graphical text editor such as gedit, Kate or Mousepad, jump to the line number from step 2, make the change and save.

verify.expect: No output. The syntax check passes. This only checks the text: the script has not been run.

warnings: bash -n checks only the syntax. It does not find wrong command names, missing files or wrong options, so the script can still fail when it runs.
A command copied from a web page may start with '$' and a space. That is the prompt from the page, not part of the command. Delete it before you run the command.
Curly quotes look like normal quotes, but the shell treats them as ordinary characters, so the command may fail later with a different error.
